opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that Huawei is a very serious competitor, but "catching up with NVIDIA" in training specifically is a much harder bar than people sometimes assume, and the gap isn't really about any single chip.

If you look at the Ascend line, the 910B and then the 910C, on paper the per-chip numbers are respectable. They're not at the level of NVIDIA's latest generation, but they're in the range where, if you're willing to throw more chips and more power at the problem, you can train frontier-ish models. And Huawei's response to being behind on the individual chip has been very rational: go big on the system level. Things like the CloudMatrix approach, where you network hundreds of Ascend chips together with a lot of optical interconnect, are basically saying, "We'll lose on efficiency per chip, we'll lose on power, but we can still deliver a large amount of aggregate compute." In China, power is comparatively less of a constraint than it is in the US, so that trade-off makes more sense there than it would here.

Where it gets hard is a few layers. The first is manufacturing. Huawei is dependent on SMIC, and SMIC is stuck without EUV lithography. They can push 7-nanometer-class and maybe a bit beyond with multi-patterning, but yields and volume are the real question. And then there's high-bandwidth memory, which is arguably an even bigger bottleneck. Training is extremely memory-bandwidth hungry, and HBM is controlled by SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron. China's domestic HBM efforts are behind, so even if you can make the logic die, feeding it is another problem. A lot of the Ascend supply has reportedly relied on stockpiled components, and that's not a sustainable footing.

The second layer is software, and this is the one I'd emphasize for training in particular. NVIDIA's moat is CUDA plus fifteen-plus years of kernels, libraries, NCCL for collective communication, and every researcher's muscle memory. Huawei has CANN and MindSpore, and they've made real progress, but when you're doing a giant training run, you hit weird numerical issues, stability issues, hardware failures, and you need a mature stack to debug those at scale. Inference is much more forgiving. You can port a model to run inference on Ascend reasonably well. Training a frontier model from scratch on it is a different level of pain, and we've seen reports of Chinese labs trying and still preferring NVIDIA hardware for their main runs when they can get it.

So my overall read is: for inference, Huawei is already viable and will take a big share of the Chinese market, especially with policy pressure pushing domestic buyers toward it. For training, they'll keep closing the gap, and the export controls ironically guarantee them a captive customer base that will grind through the software problems. But I'd think of it in terms of years behind rather than months, and the biggest determinants are not Huawei's chip design team, which is very good, but whether China can solve lithography and HBM domestically. If those break open, the picture changes a lot faster than people expect.

r001.rationale: The response discusses NVIDIA’s software ecosystem and Huawei’s reliance on SMIC and HBM suppliers, but does not identify NVIDIA as mobilizing the global supply chain to produce its highest-end AI chips.

r002.rationale: The response describes Huawei’s system-level strategy and constraints, but does not characterize its AI-chip innovation as driven by demand pressure.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you mean by "catching up," and on what time horizon.

If the question is whether Huawei can build a chip that's competitive with NVIDIA's best on raw specs, I think they can get surprisingly close, and in some ways already have. The Ascend line has been improving fast, and when you look at the numbers on paper, the gap on something like FLOPS isn't as big as people assume. The bigger constraints are on the manufacturing side. They're dependent on SMIC, they don't have access to the most advanced EUV tools, so they're paying a big penalty in yield and power efficiency to hit those numbers. And then there's HBM, high-bandwidth memory, which is really the binding constraint for training big models. If you can't get enough memory bandwidth on the chip, it doesn't matter how many FLOPS you have. That supply chain is still very hard for them.

But the thing I keep coming back to is that the chip is actually the easy part. What NVIDIA has that's really hard to replicate is the whole stack around it. CUDA, the networking, the interconnects that let you tie tens of thousands of GPUs together and actually get good utilization out of them. Training a frontier model is a systems problem, not a chip problem. And every lab that's tried to move off NVIDIA, even ones in the US with a lot of resources, has learned how painful that migration is. Huawei is trying to make up for a weaker individual chip by scaling out, putting many more accelerators in a cluster. That works in theory, but it makes the software and networking problem even harder, and that's precisely where they're furthest behind.

The other dynamic is that Huawei's customers in China don't really have a choice, which is both a blessing and a curse. Export controls mean the domestic market is increasingly theirs by default, so they get the revenue and the feedback loop from real workloads. That's genuinely valuable. DeepSeek and others have shown that Chinese labs can do a lot with constrained compute. But if you're not competing against NVIDIA head to head, you also don't get the same pressure to close the gap, and your developers are building on a software ecosystem that's isolated from where most of the open-source AI work is happening.

So my overall take is that I don't see Huawei catching NVIDIA on training in the next few years in any meaningful sense. I think the gap stays in the two-to-three year range on the hardware, and maybe wider on the systems side. Where I'd be less dismissive is inference. Inference is more forgiving, the software requirements are simpler, and that's where most of the compute demand is going anyway. If Huawei becomes the default inference platform for China, that's a huge business and a big deal strategically, even if they never win on training. And I'd be careful about underestimating them over a longer horizon. Five or ten years out, a lot of this depends on domestic lithography progress, and that's much harder to predict.

r001.rationale: The response discusses NVIDIA’s software and systems advantages but does not identify mobilizing the global supply chain as its approach to producing its highest-end AI chips.

r002.rationale: It says Huawei’s Ascend line is improving and that domestic customers provide revenue and feedback, but does not clearly characterize demand pressure as driving Huawei’s AI-chip innovation.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: can Huawei build a competitive chip, and can it build a competitive system for training large models? The second is much harder. You need memory, networking, reliable communication across thousands of chips, and software that lets researchers actually use all that hardware efficiently. NVIDIA’s advantage is that whole stack, not just the performance of an individual GPU.

Huawei doesn’t necessarily need to match NVIDIA on every dimension to become very important. If Chinese companies can’t get enough NVIDIA hardware, there’s a strong incentive to make Huawei’s platform work, even if it takes more engineering effort or more power to train the same model. That creates a customer base and a feedback loop for improving the software.

So I’d take Huawei seriously, but I’d be cautious about a specific catch-up timeline. The evidence I’d want is sustained, large-scale training: how much useful computation you get, how often the system fails, and what it costs to finish a run. A chip specification alone doesn’t answer those questions.

r001.rationale: The response describes NVIDIA’s advantage as its integrated system and software stack, but does not identify mobilizing the global supply chain as its approach to producing high-end AI chips.

r002.rationale: It says limits on access to NVIDIA hardware create a strong incentive for Chinese companies to make Huawei’s platform work, driving demand and a feedback loop for improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate building a competitive chip from building a competitive training platform. The chip matters, but at large scale you also need fast networking, reliable systems, and software that lets researchers keep thousands of accelerators working efficiently. That’s a much bigger challenge than matching a specification on paper.

Huawei has a strong incentive to make progress, and Chinese companies have a strong incentive to use its hardware. So I wouldn’t dismiss it. But I’d be cautious about predicting when it catches NVIDIA, especially because NVIDIA keeps improving too.

The milestone I’d watch is whether teams can repeatedly train frontier models on Huawei hardware with competitive costs and turnaround times. That would tell us much more than a headline about peak compute.

r001.rationale: The response discusses NVIDIA’s ongoing improvements but does not identify mobilizing the global supply chain as its approach to producing top-end AI chips.

r002.rationale: It says Huawei has a strong incentive to make progress and that Chinese companies have a strong incentive to use its hardware, conveying demand-driven pressure for Huawei to advance its AI chips.
